keyTakeaways: The NC500 remains Scotland's premier route but avoid July-August peak traffic and ride anti-clockwise for better coastal views
Scottish fuel stations can be 60+ miles apart in the Highlands – never pass one when below half tank
Pack for all seasons regardless of forecast – mountain passes can be cold even in June and layering is essential
Shoulder seasons (May-June and September) offer the best combination of weather, daylight, and lower traffic than peak summer
Single-track roads with passing places require defensive riding and concentration – watch for livestock, gravel on corners, and broken road edges
Plan realistic daily distances of 150-200 miles maximum to account for mountain passes, single-track roads, and photo stops

faq.q: When is the best time to ride motorcycle routes in Scotland?
faq.a: May, June, and September offer the best conditions – decent weather, long daylight hours, and manageable traffic. July and August have the best weather but bring heavy traffic on popular routes like the NC500, plus midges in still conditions.

faq.q: How do I deal with single-track roads on Scottish motorcycle routes?
faq.a: Watch for passing places (marked with white diamonds) and pull in to let faster traffic pass or when meeting oncoming vehicles. Ride defensively, expect livestock on the road, and watch for gravel on corners after rain.

faq.q: What motorcycle gear is essential for touring Scotland?
faq.a: Genuinely waterproof (not just resistant) outer layer, multiple clothing layers for temperature changes, heated grips for spring/autumn, and proper cold-weather gloves. Scottish weather changes rapidly, especially on mountain passes.

faq.q: How far apart are fuel stations on Highland routes?
faq.a: In remote areas, fuel stations can be 60+ miles apart with limited opening hours. Always fill up when below half tank and never assume there'll be another station soon – this catches out many touring riders.

faq.q: Can I ride the NC500 in a weekend?
faq.a: Technically yes, but you'll be rushing and miss what makes it special. The full 516-mile loop deserves minimum 4-5 days to ride properly, allowing time to enjoy the roads, scenery, and key sections like Applecross Pass.

faq.q: Do I need an adventure bike for Scottish routes?
faq.a: No – I've ridden all these routes on sports tourers, adventure bikes, and naked bikes. Main routes are fully paved and well-maintained. Adventure bikes offer comfort on longer days, but any touring-capable motorcycle works fine.

Best Motorcycle Routes in Scotland: Where to Ride in 2026

I've been riding Scottish roads for over a decade now, and I'll tell you straight – Scotland offers some of the finest motorcycling on the planet. I've toured extensively across Britain, but there's something about the Highlands that keeps pulling me back. The combination of sweeping single-track roads, dramatic coastal routes, and mountain passes creates riding that's simply unmatched.

In 2026, Scotland remains a bucket-list destination for any serious tourer. I've put together this guide based on routes I've ridden multiple times, in various conditions, so you know exactly what you're getting into. Whether you're planning a week-long tour or a long weekend blast, these routes deliver every single time.

Why Scotland is Different

Scottish motorcycling isn't just about the roads themselves – though they're brilliant – it's the entire package. You'll ride through landscapes that shift from coastal drama to mountain wilderness within an hour. The roads are generally quieter than England's, especially once you're north of Perth. I've spent entire afternoons on stunning A-roads without seeing more than a handful of vehicles.

The weather is unpredictable, sure, but that's part of the challenge. I've learned to pack for all four seasons regardless of the forecast. The reward for accepting this uncertainty is riding through landscapes that change character completely depending on the light and conditions. A road I've ridden in mist one year becomes an entirely different experience in bright sunshine the next.

The North Coast 500: Still the Headline Act

Let's address the elephant in the room first. The NC500 has become incredibly popular – perhaps too popular in peak summer – but it remains essential riding. I've completed this 516-mile loop numerous times, and despite the increased traffic, it's still spectacular.

The route circles the northern Highlands, starting and finishing in Inverness. What makes it special is the variety: you'll tackle the western coastal sections with their technical bends and stunning sea views, then swing across to the north coast's more exposed, sweeping roads, before dropping down the dramatic east coast back to Inverness.

My advice? Ride it anti-clockwise. You'll tackle the western section's tighter roads while you're fresh, and the coastal views are better on the left side. More importantly, avoid July and August if possible. I rode it in early June 2025 and traffic was manageable. By late July, motorhomes were causing queues on single-track sections.

The standout sections for me are the Applecross Pass (Bealach na Bà), which climbs to 626 metres with hairpins that'll have you grinning inside your helmet, and the run from Durness to Tongue along the north coast – wide, flowing roads with views that make you want to stop every few miles.

For a detailed breakdown of tackling this route properly, I've written a complete guide at NC500 Complete that covers accommodation, fuel stops, and section-by-section riding notes.

The A82: Glasgow to Fort William

This is one of Scotland's classic ribbons of tarmac, and I've lost count of how many times I've ridden it. The A82 follows the western edge of Loch Lomond, then cuts through Glen Coe before arriving in Fort William. It's roughly 100 miles of varied riding that showcases exactly why Scotland works so well for motorcycles.

The southern section past Loch Lomond can be busy, especially with weekend traffic from Glasgow, but once you're past Tarbet, it opens up beautifully. The Glen Coe section is genuinely dramatic – towering mountains on either side, sweeping bends, and a surface that's generally good (though watch for gravel after heavy rain).

I always stop at the Green Welly Stop in Tyndrum for fuel and a brew. It's a proper biker-friendly spot where you can check your route and grab supplies. The final run into Fort William offers stunning views of Ben Nevis when the weather's clear.

One word of caution: this road can be lethal in winter conditions. I attempted it in early March once and turned back – the ice patches and snow made it genuinely dangerous. Stick to April through October unless you're very experienced in winter riding.

The A87: From Fort William to Skye

Continuing west from Fort William, the A87 takes you through some of the most photogenic riding in Britain. This route heads to Kyle of Lochalsh and the bridge to Skye, passing through Invergarry and alongside Loch Cluanie.

The section around the Five Sisters of Kintail is breathtaking. The road sweeps through the glen with mountains rising dramatically on both sides. I've ridden this in morning mist, afternoon sunshine, and during a summer storm – it's magnificent in all conditions, though obviously more challenging when visibility drops.

Once you cross to Skye, you're in for a treat. The island offers fantastic riding, from the dramatic Trotternish Peninsula in the north to the Cuillin mountains in the south. The roads are generally single-track with passing places, which means you need to ride defensively and be prepared to stop frequently. I detailed this entire route in Island to Highlands, including the best places to stay on Skye itself.

The A93: Cairngorms Mountain Road

This route from Blairgowrie to Braemar includes Britain's highest public road at the Cairnwell Pass, reaching 670 metres. I love this road for its complete change of scenery – you start in relatively gentle countryside and end up in proper mountain terrain.

The climb to the ski centre at Glenshee is a series of sweeping bends that reward smooth riding. The views from the top are expansive when clear. I've ridden this in June and still encountered snow patches on the verges. The descent into Braemar is equally enjoyable, with good sightlines and a well-maintained surface.

Make time to explore beyond the main route. The A939 from Ballater over the Lecht is another high pass worth riding, though it's more exposed and can be properly cold even in summer. I always pack an extra layer specifically for these mountain crossings.

The A832: Wester Ross Coastal Route

This is one of my absolute favourite roads in Scotland, yet it doesn't get the attention it deserves. The A832 loops around Wester Ross, taking in Gairloch and some stunning coastal scenery that rivals anything on the NC500 but with significantly less traffic.

Starting from the A835 at Gorstan, the road winds through wild landscape to Gairloch, then hugs the coast southward before turning inland to Kinlochewe. The coastal section between Gairloch and Redpoint is particularly special – single-track with passing places, stunning sea views, and barely any traffic midweek.

I rode this in September 2024 and had entire sections to myself. The evening light on the sea was incredible. Just be aware that single-track riding requires concentration – you need to spot passing places well in advance and be ready to pull in for faster vehicles or oncoming traffic.

Scottish riding is about embracing the conditions rather than fighting them. Pack for weather variety, fuel up whenever you see a station, and give yourself time to stop and absorb the scenery. The best routes can't be rushed.

The A708: Moffat to Selkirk

Not everything needs to be in the Highlands. The A708 through the Southern Uplands is a cracking ride that's often overlooked. This 50-mile stretch takes you through the Grey Mare's Tail waterfall area and over some proper elevation changes.

The road is technical enough to keep you engaged but not so demanding that you can't enjoy the scenery. I particularly like the section around St. Mary's Loch – it's peaceful, scenic, and the road surface is generally excellent. The Grey Mare's Tail is worth a brief stop if you need to stretch your legs.

This route works brilliantly as a day ride from the central belt or as part of a longer tour connecting into the Lake District or heading north into the Highlands. I've used it numerous times as a shakedown ride when testing new gear before longer tours.

Essential Gear for Scottish Routes

Scottish weather demands proper kit. I learned this the hard way years ago when I underestimated how cold it could get in May. These days, my Scottish touring setup always includes a proper waterproof layer – not just "water resistant" but genuinely waterproof. I've had good experiences with gear from SportsBikeShop, particularly their range of touring jackets designed for British conditions.

Layer effectively. I typically ride with a base layer, mid-layer fleece, and my jacket. On mountain passes, I'll add a thermal under-layer even in June. It sounds excessive until you're at 600 metres in a 40mph wind and grateful for every layer.

Heated grips or gloves are worth considering if you're touring in spring or autumn. I resisted for years, then finally fitted heated grips – they've transformed early and late season riding. Cold hands affect your control and enjoyment more than any other single factor.

For navigation, I use a combination of a tank bag with a map pocket and a phone mount with GPS. Signal can be patchy in the Highlands, so download offline maps. I've had entire days in Wester Ross without any mobile signal whatsoever.

Practical Planning for 2026

Fuel stations can be sparse in the Highlands. I never pass a fuel station if I'm below half a tank. Seriously. I've seen riders caught out assuming there'll be another station "soon" – in some areas, soon means 60 miles. Keep your tank topped up.

Accommodation books up fast for peak season, especially along the NC500. If you're touring July or August, book months ahead. I prefer shoulder seasons anyway – May, June, and September offer the best combination of weather, daylight hours, and available accommodation.

Midges are real and they're absolutely vicious in still conditions, particularly July and August. They're attracted to dark colours and carbon dioxide from your breath. If you're camping, pitch in windy spots – midges can't fly in even moderate wind. I carry midge repellent as standard gear from May through September.

Use build route to plan your daily distances. Scottish miles take longer than English miles – single-track roads, mountain passes, and stopping to take photos all add time. I typically plan around 150-200 miles per day maximum, which gives me time to actually enjoy the riding rather than rushing between points.

Road Conditions and Seasonal Considerations

Scottish roads are generally well-maintained, but they're not perfect. Single-track roads can have broken edges, gravel accumulates on corners after rain, and livestock genuinely do wander onto the road. I've had to emergency brake for sheep more times than I can count.

Spring (April-May) offers longer days, less traffic, and spectacular scenery as everything greens up. Temperatures are cool but manageable with proper gear. Some higher passes may still have occasional closures due to snow early in the season.

Summer (June-August) brings the best weather but also the worst traffic, particularly on the NC500. Daylight extends until nearly 11pm in June, which is brilliant for evening rides. This is midge season though, so be prepared.

Autumn (September-October) is my favourite time to ride Scotland. The traffic drops dramatically after schools return, the autumn colours are stunning, and the weather is often settled. Days are shorter, so plan accordingly, but the quality of riding is superb.

Winter (November-March) is challenging. Daylight is limited, temperatures are low, and mountain passes can be closed. I only ride Scotland in winter for specific short trips, and I check conditions obsessively before setting out. Ice is a genuine danger on higher roads.

Connecting Routes Together

The beauty of Scottish touring is how easily routes connect. I often combine the A82 to Fort William with the A87 to Skye, then head north to join the western section of the NC500, before cutting across to the east coast and returning south via the Cairngorms. This creates a week-long tour that covers the absolute highlights.

For route planning that considers your riding style, fuel stops, and accommodation options, check out plan trip which helps you build realistic daily itineraries. I wish I'd had this tool when I was starting out – it would have saved me from several overly-ambitious days where I arrived at my accommodation exhausted.

Consider loop routes rather than out-and-back trips. Riding the same road in reverse doesn't give you much new scenery. Scotland's road network allows you to create circular routes that maximize variety. Even a long weekend gives you enough time for a satisfying loop if you plan efficiently.

Where to Stay

I mix my accommodation between small hotels, B&Bs, and the occasional campsite. Scottish B&Bs are generally biker-friendly and offer excellent value. Many provide secure parking and will let you dry gear if you've been caught in rain.

Camping gives you flexibility but requires more planning in Scotland – wild camping is legal in most areas, but you need to follow the Scottish Outdoor Access Code. Designated campsites are plentiful and usually have facilities suitable for touring riders.

Fort William, Inverness, and Portree on Skye make good base towns for multi-night stays, allowing day rides without moving your accommodation. Alternatively, keep moving and stay somewhere different each night to cover maximum ground.

Food and Refreshments

Don't expect services everywhere. In remote areas, there might be nothing between villages. I always carry emergency snacks – energy bars, nuts, and plenty of water. Dehydration affects your riding more than you realize.

When you find a café or pub, use it. These establishments are lifelines in remote areas. I've had brilliant conversations with other riders and locals at small Highland cafés, getting tips about roads I'd never have found otherwise.

Pack a thermos with hot coffee or tea if you're riding mountain passes. Stopping for a brew with a mountain view is one of touring's genuine pleasures, and you can't always rely on finding somewhere open.

Getting There and Back

From England, the ride into Scotland via the A74(M) and M74 is straightforward but not particularly scenic. I usually push through to Glasgow or Edinburgh, then start the proper touring from there. Alternatively, the A68 through the Borders is slower but more interesting.

If you're short on time, consider riding up one route and returning via another. The A1 up the east coast is faster but less interesting than western routes. I've done Edinburgh to Inverness via the A9 in under four hours when pushed for time, but it's not the most rewarding riding.

Ferry options exist for returning if you've ridden to the islands. The ferries from Skye, or from Mull and other western isles, can make interesting alternatives to retracing your route entirely by road.

Final Thoughts and Next Steps

Scotland offers motorcycling that stands comparison with anywhere in Europe. The roads are challenging enough to be engaging without being terrifying, the scenery is world-class, and there's enough variety to satisfy any touring rider's preferences. I've ridden Alps passes and Mediterranean coastal roads, but I keep coming back to Scotland because it combines great riding with accessibility and value.

Your 2026 Scottish tour starts with proper planning. Use top 20 motorcycle roads UK to see how these Scottish routes compare with riding elsewhere in Britain. Then make your route decisions, book accommodation for peak season, and sort your gear well in advance.

The routes I've covered here represent my personal favourites from hundreds of miles of Scottish riding. They're proven routes that deliver regardless of your experience level or bike type. I've ridden them on sports tourers, adventure bikes, and naked bikes – they work on anything.

Check your bike thoroughly before heading north. Scottish routes can be demanding, and being stuck with a mechanical issue in a remote Highland glen is nobody's idea of fun. Fresh tyres, good brakes, and reliable lights are essentials.

Most importantly, give yourself time. Scottish routes reward riders who aren't rushing. Build in extra days if possible, accept that weather might alter your plans, and embrace the adventure. Some of my best touring memories come from unexpected detours and weather-forced changes to my carefully planned routes.

Now sort your dates, get your gear together, and I'll see you up there. Scotland in 2026 is waiting, and trust me – it's worth every mile of the ride north.
